questions.q: Which earlier chapter is described as the most direct ancestor of Lesson 29's test and Lesson 31's incident?
options: Chapter 2, Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
Chapter 5, Adversarial Examples and Evasion Attacks
Chapter 4, Model Extraction and Inversion Attacks
Chapter 3, Data Poisoning and Training-Time Attacks
questions.explain: Direct and indirect prompt injection, and the idea that input sanitization alone isn't enough, is exactly what Lesson 29 tested for and what ProcureAssist lacked.

questions.q: What specifically went wrong architecturally in Lesson 31's ProcureAssist case study, as this review restates it?
options: The model's training data had been poisoned
An attacker directly logged into the agent's console
The company used the wrong cloud provider
ProcureAssist's blast radius included a tool (approve_purchase_order) it never should have reached from a document-summarization session
questions.explain: The review ties the incident back to Chapter 6's blast-radius and privilege-separation concepts, not a model flaw or an external attacker.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how many Expert Specialization courses does this one sit alongside, and in what order can they be taken?
options: Four total, and they must be taken in the exact order listed in the path
Two total, taken in a fixed order after this one
Four total -- this course plus three others -- buildable on the same Advanced-stage foundation and takeable in any order
This is the only Expert Specialization course in the path
questions.explain: The four Expert Specialization courses (this one, Digital Forensics & Malware Analysis, Ethical Hacking/Pentesting/Purple Team, and Enterprise Security Architecture/GRC) build on the Advanced stage but not on each other.

questions.q: What is Category 3 of the Lesson 30 checklist, and which chapter does it come from?
options: Adversarial robustness testing, from Chapter 5
Rate limiting and query monitoring for model extraction, from Chapter 4
Prompt injection defenses, from Chapter 2
Governance and red-teaming, from Chapter 7
questions.explain: Chapter 4's model extraction defenses -- rate limiting and query monitoring -- became Category 3 of the checklist, guarding against a feature leaking its model through an unmonitored API.

questions.q: According to this lesson's closing summary, what did this capstone actually prove about securing an AI application?
options: That a security review is one single pass/fail test run once before launch
That a model behaving correctly at every step guarantees a safe system
That input sanitization alone is always sufficient

That a security review spans an authorized assessment, a category-based checklist, and architectural controls -- because correct model behavior alone can't prevent an incident without privilege separation and human oversight
questions.explain: The capstone's throughline is that security is a structured process, not a single check, and that architecture -- not just model behavior -- is what actually prevents incidents like Lesson 31's.
